overview: This 650-page file documents the rapid tightening of American and Allied economic pressure on Japan in mid-1941. Its central subject is petroleum: public letters, congressional inquiries, editorials, cartoons, company representations, and State Department memoranda debate continued oil exports to Japan amid domestic conservation appeals and Japan’s war in China. Alongside this controversy, diplomatic, consular, naval, FBI, and commercial reports trace Japanese efforts to obtain rubber, iron ore, scrap metal, cotton, platinum, tungsten, manganese, cobalt, and other strategic materials across Southeast Asia and Latin America. Statistical studies and policy memoranda assess Japan’s dependence on imports, the operation of export licensing, and the danger that an embargo might provoke Japanese expansion or war, while later documents record the freezing of Japanese assets and stricter petroleum controls.
interest: The file is unusually valuable because it places high-level strategic calculation beside a large body of public protest, revealing the political pressure behind economic sanctions as well as officials’ reluctance to impose them too quickly. Detailed reports on Japanese purchasing networks, shipping, financing, stockpiling, and import dependence allow historians to reconstruct the global material foundations of Japan’s war economy. The repeated contrast between domestic “gasless Sundays” and tankers carrying oil to Japan also offers a vivid study of how newspaper coverage, cartoons, civic activism, congressional mediation, commercial interests, and foreign-policy secrecy interacted immediately before the Pacific War.
